extracted.intended_audience: new and intermediate creative writers (fiction and narrative prose writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for applying the "show, don't tell" technique in fiction and narrative writing, including when to prefer showing vs telling and tactics to convert telling into showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick definition of "Show, don't tell"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Show, don’t tell" is a creative writing technique that allows the reader to experience the story through actions, senses, and other vivid details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete sensory details, actions, and specific moments to immerse readers in the story rather than simply stating facts or emotions (i.e., avoid plain exposition or summary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show vs Tell (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling (exposition/narrative summary) states facts; showing uses specific details so readers feel like they experienced the event alongside characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you 'tell' a fact (e.g., 'Mary was embarrassed') it communicates only the fact; when you 'show' through behavior and physical signs (e.g., flushed cheeks, hiding a test) you create a vivid, engaging experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use showing to engross readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing allows you to create a vivid picture in your reader’s mind that will engross them in your writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatic scenes and vivid details to keep readers engaged — the article compares being told about an event to hearing a friend describe a breakup versus watching a movie of it. Use showing for moments where you want sustained reader attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave room for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing lets readers draw their own conclusions and form a deeper relationship with the text rather than having everything spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid naming every thought and feeling of characters; provide clues (actions, dialogue, sensory detail) so readers can infer motivations and emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey deeper meaning through concrete detail
rubrics_metrics.description: "Show, don’t tell" increases the density of meaning by demonstrating what emotions or traits look like, rather than labeling them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show emotions via body language, actions, and context to develop characters more deeply; examples: show overprotectiveness through repeated specific behaviors, show devotion through repeated concrete actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple sensory details for setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Show setting with sensory descriptions (sight, sound, smell, texture) rather than abstract labels like 'scary' or 'beautiful'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine visual metaphors (branches like gnarled hands), sounds (leaves crunch), and smells (mildew, decay) to immerse readers in place; sensory layering strengthens immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Camera Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself, 'Can a camera see this?' If not, you may be telling instead of showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make scenes 'camera ready' by adding concrete details a camera (and by extension a reader) could register: locations, objects, sounds, tastes, textures, and smells. Use the test to find areas that need more showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement more dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is inherently a form of showing because characters' words reveal feelings, status, and relationships without explicit naming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use how characters speak (stutters, verbosity, tone, choice of words) to reveal emotion, social dynamics, and subtext rather than summarizing feelings in narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on actions and body language
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate traits and emotions through characters' actions and physical cues instead of labeling them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show a liar via behaviors and choices, show prowess through described exploits, and practice conveying emotions without naming them (e.g., guilt shown by insomnia or reparative actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell first, then show (drafting workflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: It's acceptable in early drafts to 'tell' to lay out plot and beats; during revision, convert tells into shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use telling to get the scene structure down quickly, then revisit and add sensory details, actions, and dialogue to transform tells into effective showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use telling for pacing and unimportant information
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling is useful when describing something unimportant or when showing would bog down pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve showing for moments that need immersion; use telling to move time forward quickly or summarize routine events to keep narrative momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to tell: Transition scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions (travel, unremarkable time passing) are appropriate places to tell rather than show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nothing eventful occurs en route or during a span of time, summarize ('A month later…') instead of dramatizing each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to tell: Mundane scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyday mundane actions that add little to story interest can be told succinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long descriptions of trivial actions (e.g., getting dressed); a simple line like 'She got dressed' is often sufficient unless the moment has narrative significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to tell: Repeated scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't show repeated iterations of the same event; summarize repetitive occurrences and save dramatization for the climactic instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: summarize earlier rounds of a tournament and fully show only the decisive round to avoid reader fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance showing and telling based on narrative needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'show, don't tell' rule is a guideline, not an absolute; choose showing or telling based on engagement, pacing, and importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use showing to increase engagement, nuance, and depth; use telling to maintain pace, skip unimportant detail, or summarize repeated/unremarkable events. Exercise judgment to find the right mix.
